---
title: "Question 3: Would Its Headline Finding Survive a Push?"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/common.R")
fr <- readRDS("data/fragility.rds")
cal <- readRDS("data/calibration.rds")
fc <- readRDS("data/forecast.rds")
cv <- fr$curve
b <- fr$base
ps <- fr$plus_size
sd_or <- fr$seed_or
fal <- fr$falsifyr
fal_tab <- as.data.frame(fal$attacks)
full <- fc$results[1, ]
sh <- fr$deletion_shares
raw_top <- cal$reliability[cal$reliability$score == "Raw VendorScore", ]
raw_top <- raw_top[which.max(raw_top$bin), ]
cm <- cal$ci[cal$ci$variant == "Isotonic overlay" & cal$ci$metric == "brier", ]
sgn <- function(x, d = 5) sub("^-", "−", formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f"))
brier_chg <- cal$metrics["Isotonic overlay", "brier"] - cal$metrics["Raw VendorScore", "brier"]
```

## The question

NorthPoint built its own logistic regression, the bank's incident-association model, from
its panel. Its headline: vendors without a current SOC 2 Type II report have about twice
the odds of an incident (odds ratio `r num(b$or)`, vendor-clustered 95% interval `r num(b$low)` to `r num(b$high)`). That finding
now supports a contract policy. How small a change makes it disappear?

## Method in brief

**Pre-registered definition of a "kill":** the no-SOC-2 coefficient loses statistical
significance at the 5% level using vendor-clustered standard errors (`sandwich::vcovCL`,
Wald z). Ordinary standard errors ignore within-vendor dependence and may overstate precision.

A *specification curve* re-estimates the odds ratio across 16 logit models (so every estimate
is an odds ratio): include or omit vendor size, prior incidents and financial health, with or
without trimming the slowest 1% of patch latencies. A *greedy deletion search* then removes,
one at a time, the incident rows that most support the estimate, from the analysis dataset
only; recorded lagged history is kept. Both are bounded searches, not proofs of what is smallest.

The `falsifyr` package supplies the refits and a supplementary within-model attack run.^[[`falsifyr`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=falsifyr) 1.0.0: `refit_model()` performs each specification refit; `attack()` (term `no_soc2`, intensity "normal", seed 34, kill rule p over alpha) ran 20 attacks: 19 survived, one unavailable. Its configured routine did not evaluate the added-control specification under our vendor-clustered inference rule, so we implemented that check separately.]

## Findings

```{r}
#| label: fig-speccurve
#| fig-cap: "No-SOC-2 odds ratio across 16 logit specifications, ordered by size, with 95% vendor-clustered intervals. Dashed line: data-generating conditional OR, 1.25."
#| fig-alt: "Dot-and-interval plot of 16 odds ratios in two clusters: about 1.3 with vendor size included, about 2.0 to 2.4 without it, with a horizontal line at 1.25."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
cv$label <- ifelse(cv$vendor_size, "Vendor size included", "Vendor size omitted")
ggplot(cv, aes(rank, or, colour = label)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = fr$true_or, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), size = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(okabe_ito[c("blue", "vermillion")])) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.8, 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3), labels = c("0.8", "1", "1.25", "1.5", "2", "3")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Specification (ordered by odds ratio)",
       y = "Odds ratio for no SOC 2 (log scale)", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** Each dot is one reasonable way of building the model; height is the
estimated increase in the odds of an incident for vendors without SOC 2, and 1 means no
effect. The vertical line is the plausible range. The dashed line is the generator's
conditional odds ratio, known because the data are simulated.

**What the plot tells you.** The dots form two groups, split by one decision: vendor size.
Larger vendors are more likely to hold SOC 2 and are safer, so leaving size out credits SOC 2
with that safety. Closeness to 1.25 does not prove a causal model has been recovered.
:::

All `r sum(!cv$vendor_size & cv$significant)` specifications without vendor size are significant (odds ratios `r num(min(cv$or[!cv$vendor_size]))` to
`r num(max(cv$or[!cv$vendor_size]))`); none of the `r sum(cv$vendor_size)` that include it is (`r num(min(cv$or[cv$vendor_size]))` to `r num(max(cv$or[cv$vendor_size]))`). Adding vendor size alone
takes the estimate to `r num(ps$or)` (interval `r num(ps$low)` to `r num(ps$high)`, p = `r pval(ps$p)`) with no data removed.
This concerns the association; it does not show that SOC 2 has no effect.

```{r}
#| label: fig-kill
#| fig-cap: "Greedy deletion search: clustered p-value as supportive incident rows are deleted. The diamond is the size-adjusted model with nothing deleted."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of p-value rising as rows are deleted, crossing 0.05 at the point marked, and a diamond above 0.05 at zero deletions for the model with vendor size."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
dp <- fr$deletion_path
ggplot(dp, aes(step, p)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_line(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = okabe_ito[["blue"]], size = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(step = 0, p = ps$p), shape = 18, size = 5,
             colour = okabe_ito[["vermillion"]]) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Incident vendor-months deleted (greedy search)",
       y = "Clustered p-value (log scale)")
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the plot.** The blue line removes, one at a time, incidents at vendors
without SOC 2 that most support the finding, and tracks how convincing the result stays.
Higher means weaker evidence; above the dashed line it is no longer statistically
significant. The diamond is the size-adjusted result, with no rows removed.

**What the plot tells you.** This is an adversarial stress test, not data cleaning. The two
routes to the 5% line are different kinds of distance, so they should not be compared by counting.
:::

The search found a successful perturbation, within its budget of `r fr$budget` deletions, at
`r fr$kill_rows` deleted rows: `r pct(sh["of_rows"], 2)` of all `r format(fr$n_rows, big.mark = ",")` rows, `r pct(sh["of_incidents"], 1)` of all `r fr$n_incidents` incidents and
`r pct(sh["of_eligible"], 1)` of the `r fr$n_eligible` eligible supportive incidents. A greedy search gives
an upper bound on the smallest such change, and post-search p-values are diagnostics, not
fresh tests. `falsifyr` found no kill in its run (verdict `r tolower(fal$verdict)`), which is not proof of robustness.

**Seed sensitivity.** Each seed generates a different synthetic dataset, so this is a
Monte Carlo repeatability check, not a perturbation of the bank's data. We re-ran the
generator for seeds 1 to 40, with the same clustered baseline. The omitted-size odds ratio ranged from `r num(min(sd_or$naive_or))` to `r num(max(sd_or$naive_or))` (median `r num(median(sd_or$naive_or))`), significant in `r sum(sd_or$naive_p < 0.05)` of 40
runs. With size included it ranged from `r num(min(sd_or$adj_or))` to `r num(max(sd_or$adj_or))` (median `r num(median(sd_or$adj_or))`), significant in `r sum(sd_or$adj_p < 0.05)`. These counts
are descriptive and imprecise. Seed 34 was chosen during development because it illustrates the
intended patterns so its p-values are not an
unbiased experiment. The upward bias from omitting size is repeatable; the exact "2×" is not.

## So what

The "2× odds" headline reflects confounding in this simulator, not a robust effect of
SOC 2: the size-adjusted estimate is `r num(ps$or)` (`r num(ps$low)` to `r num(ps$high)`), which is also compatible with a sizeable effect. The bank's own model
was built to describe associations, then reused to support a contract policy.
The April 17, 2026 interagency [*Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management*](https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13a.pdf)
(Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC) flags use beyond a model's intended purpose (§IV, Model Use), and
describes effective challenge (§III) and testing with alternative assumptions (§IV). The challenge here
was one added variable. This is partial validation too, and a robust association would still not
be a causal effect.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-scorecard
#| tbl-cap: "Series scorecard: measured results at NorthPoint, and responses in the guidance's vocabulary (measured result and decision kept separate)."
score <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Calibration", "Forecast dominance", "Fragility"),
  Question = c("Honest probabilities?", "Beats a simple model?", "Robust headline?"),
  `Measured result` = c(
    sprintf("Raw top group predicted %s, observed %s. Isotonic overlay changes Brier by %s (%s to %s); gains small and unclear.",
            pct(raw_top$predicted), pct(raw_top$observed), sgn(brier_chg), sgn(cm$diff_low), sgn(cm$diff_high)),
    sprintf("MSE %s lower than the 12-month average; DM p = %s (n = 18): no detectable advantage.",
            pct(1 - full$mse_vs / full$mse_naive, 0), pval(full$dm_p)),
    sprintf("Odds ratio %s becomes %s (p = %s) when vendor size is added; one added variable removes significance.",
            num(b$or), num(ps$or), num(ps$p))),
  `Suggested response` = c(
    "Do not approve the tested overlay for routine use yet; investigate, keep the existing process under documented controls, validate any replacement on later outcomes.",
    "Closer monitoring; raise with vendor; ask for development evidence; keep contingency plan.",
    "Limit use: do not use this association alone to infer the effect of requiring SOC 2; document the exception."),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(score)
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** One row per question: what we measured at NorthPoint, and the
action sound practice suggests, in the guidance's vocabulary. An overlay adjusts a model's
output without changing the model; limits on use restrict what a result may be used for.

**What the table tells you.** None of the three tests found anything clean, and none, alone,
argues for scrapping VendorScore. The weakest item is the bank's own finding.
:::

## Committee action

Sound practice suggests documenting the SOC 2 finding as an exception (§VI) and
analysing its new use before relying on it (§IV). Do not use this association alone to infer the effect of requiring SOC 2: contract
requirements need business, legal and control evidence. The guidance does not prescribe this.
